scenes.say: In just four years, one war killed around twenty million people and redrew the map of the world. This is World War One, explained.
By 1914, Europe was a powder keg. The great powers had split into two rival alliances, and each promised to defend its friends.
scenes.sub: a powder keg waiting for a spark

scenes.say: June twenty eighth, 1914. In Sarajevo, a young Bosnian Serb named Gavrilo Princip shoots Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to Austria-Hungary's throne.
scenes.sub: an archduke is shot in Sarajevo

scenes.say: Austria-Hungary declares war on Serbia. Russia backs Serbia. Germany backs Austria, and invades Belgium to reach France. Britain joins in. In about a week, Europe is at war.
scenes.sub: one war becomes a world war

scenes.say: Both sides expected a short war, over by Christmas. Instead, the Western Front froze into trenches stretching from the North Sea to Switzerland.
scenes.sub: from the North Sea to Switzerland

scenes.say: Soldiers lived in mud, with rats and disease. Between the trenches lay no man's land, where machine guns cut down almost any attack.
On the first day of the Battle of the Somme alone, July first, 1916, the British Army suffered about fifty seven thousand casualties.
scenes.sub: British casualties in a single day

scenes.say: To break the deadlock, armies turned to terrifying new weapons. Poison gas was used on a large scale from 1915.
scenes.sub: used on a large scale from 1915

scenes.say: And in September 1916, British tanks rolled into battle for the very first time.
scenes.sub: first used in battle at the Somme

scenes.say: In 1917, everything shifted. The United States joined the war, while Russia, torn apart by revolution, dropped out.
In the spring of 1918, Germany launched one last huge attack. It failed. With fresh American troops arriving, the Allies pushed back.
At eleven in the morning on November eleventh, 1918, the guns finally fell silent.
Around twenty million soldiers and civilians were dead.
In 1919, exactly five years after the shots in Sarajevo, the Treaty of Versailles blamed Germany and ordered it to pay huge reparations.
The anger it caused helped set the stage for World War Two, just twenty years later. That is why historians say one war led straight to the next.
